{{Short description|Measure in mathematical analysis}}
{{More footnotes needed|date=June 2020}}
In [[mathematical analysis]], a '''Young measure''' is a parameterized [[measure (mathematics)|measure]] that is associated with certain subsequences of a given bounded sequence of measurable functions. They are a quantification of the oscillation effect of the sequence in the limit.  Young measures have applications in the [[calculus of variations]], especially models from material science, and the study of [[nonlinear]] [[partial differential equations]], as well as in various [[optimization]] (or [[optimal control]] problems).  They are named after [[Laurence Chisholm Young]] who invented them, already in 1937 in one dimension (curves) and later in higher dimensions in 1942.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Young|first=L. C.|date=1942|title=Generalized Surfaces in the Calculus of Variations|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1968882|journal=Annals of Mathematics|volume=43|issue=1|pages=84–103|doi=10.2307/1968882|jstor=1968882 |issn=0003-486X|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

Young measures provide a solution to [[Hilbert's twentieth problem|Hilbert’s twentieth problem]], as a broad class of problems in the calculus of variations have solutions in the form of Young measures.<ref name=":0">[https://web.archive.org/web/20220127215235/https://webspace.science.uu.nl/~balde101/lyoungm.pdf Balder, Erik J. "Lectures on Young measures." ''Cahiers de Mathématiques de la Décision'' 9517 (1995).]</ref>

==Definition==

=== Intuition ===
Young constructed the Young measure in order to complete sets of ordinary curves in the calculus of variations. That is, Young measures are "generalized curves".<ref name=":0" />

Consider the problem of <math>\min_u I(u) = \int_0^1 (u'(x)^2-1)^2 +u(x)^2 dx</math>, where <math>u</math> is a function such that <math>u(0) = u(1) = 0</math>, and continuously differentiable. It is clear that we should pick <math>u</math> to have value close to zero, and its slope close to <math>\pm 1</math>. That is, the curve should be a tight jagged line hugging close to the x-axis. No function can reach the minimum value of <math>I = 0</math>, but we can construct a sequence of functions <math>u_1, u_2, \dots</math> that are increasingly jagged, such that <math>I(u_n) \to 0</math>.

The pointwise limit <math>\lim u_n</math> is identically zero, but the pointwise limit <math>\lim_n u_n'</math> does not exist. Instead, it is a fine mist that has half of its weight on <math>+1</math>, and the other half on <math>-1</math>.

Suppose that <math>F</math> is a functional defined by <math>F(u) = \int_0^1 f(t, u(t), u'(t))dt</math>, where <math>f</math> is continuous, then <math display="block">\lim_n F(u_n) = \frac 12 \int_0^1 f(t, 0, -1)dt + \frac 12 \int_0^1 f(t, 0, +1)dt</math>so in the [[Weak derivative|weak sense]], we can define <math>\lim_n u_n</math> to be a "function" whose value is zero and whose derivative is <math>\frac 12 \delta_{-1} + \frac 12 \delta_{+1}</math>. In particular, it would mean that <math>I(\lim_n u_n ) = 0</math>.

===Motivation===

The definition of Young measures is motivated by the following theorem: Let ''m'', ''n'' be arbitrary positive integers, let <math>U</math>  be an open bounded subset of <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math> and <math>\{ f_k \}_{k=1}^\infty</math> be a bounded sequence in <math>L^p (U,\mathbb{R}^m)</math>{{clarify|date=May 2022|reason=Which ''p'' -- for all ''p'' in [1,+infty]? Please quantify ''p''.}}. Then there exists a subsequence <math>\{ f_{k_j} \}_{j=1}^\infty \subset \{ f_k \}_{k=1}^\infty</math> and for almost every <math>x \in U</math> a [[Borel measure|Borel probability measure]] <math>\nu_x</math> on <math>\mathbb{R}^m</math> such that for each <math>F \in C(\mathbb{R}^m)</math> we have 
:<math>F \circ f_{k_j}(x) {\rightharpoonup} \int_{\mathbb{R}^m} F(y)d\nu_x(y)</math>
[[Weak topology|weakly]] in <math>L^p(U)</math> if the limit exists (or weakly* in  <math>L^\infty (U)</math> in case of <math>p=+\infty</math>). The measures <math>\nu_x</math> are called ''the Young measures generated by the sequence <math>\{ f_{k_j} \}_{j=1}^\infty</math>''.

A partial converse is also true: If for each <math>x\in U</math> we have a Borel measure <math>\nu_x</math> on <math>\mathbb R^m</math> such that <math>\int_U\int_{\R^m}\|y\|^pd\nu_x(y)dx<+\infty</math>, then there exists a sequence <math>\{f_k\}_{k=1}^\infty\subseteq L^p(U,\mathbb R^m)</math>, bounded in <math> L^p(U,\mathbb R^m)</math>, that has the same weak convergence property as above.

More generally, for any [[Carathéodory function]] <math>G(x,A) : U\times R^m \to R</math>, the limit
:<math>\lim_{j\to \infty} \int_{U} G(x,f_j(x)) \  d x,</math>
if it exists, will be given by<ref>{{Cite book|last=Pedregal|first=Pablo|title=Parametrized measures and variational principles|date=1997|publisher=Birkhäuser Verlag|isbn=978-3-0348-8886-8|location=Basel|oclc=812613013}}</ref>
:<math>\int_{U} \int_{\R^m} G(x,A) \ d \nu_x(A) \ dx</math>.

Young's original idea in the case <math>G\in C_0(U \times \R^m) </math> was to consider for each integer <math>j\ge1</math>  the uniform measure, let's say <math>\Gamma_j:= (id ,f_j)_\sharp L ^d\llcorner U,</math> concentrated on graph of the function <math>f_j.</math> (Here, <math>L ^d\llcorner U</math> is the restriction of the [[Lebesgue measure]] on <math>U.</math>) By taking the weak* limit of these measures as elements of <math>C_0(U \times \R^m)^\star,</math> we have 
:<math>\langle\Gamma_j, G\rangle = \int_{U} G(x,f_j(x)) \  d x \to  \langle\Gamma ,G\rangle,</math>
where <math>\Gamma</math> is the mentioned weak limit. After a disintegration of the  measure <math>\Gamma</math> on the product space <math>\Omega \times \R^m,</math> we get the parameterized measure <math>\nu_x</math>.

===General definition===

Let <math>m,n</math> be arbitrary positive integers, let <math>U</math> be an open and bounded subset of <math>\mathbb R^n</math>, and let <math>p\geq 1</math>. A ''Young measure'' (with finite ''p''-moments) is a family of Borel probability measures <math>\{\nu_x : x\in U\}</math> on <math>\mathbb R^m</math> such that <math>\int_U\int_{\R^m}
\|y\|^p d\nu_x(y)dx<+\infty</math>.

== Examples ==

=== Pointwise converging sequence ===
A trivial example of Young measure is when the sequence <math>f_n</math> is bounded in <math>L^\infty(U, \mathbb{R}^n )</math> and converges pointwise almost everywhere in <math>U</math> to a function <math>f</math>. The Young measure is then the [[Dirac measure]]
:<math>\nu_x = \delta_{f(x)}, \quad x \in U.</math>
Indeed, by [[dominated convergence theorem]], <math>F(f_n(x))</math> converges weakly* in <math> L^\infty (U) </math> to
:<math> F(f(x)) = \int F(y) \, \text{d} \delta_{f(x)}  </math>
for any <math> F \in C(\mathbb{R}^n)</math>.

=== Sequence of sines ===
A less trivial example is a sequence
:<math> f_n(x) = \sin (n x), \quad x \in (0,2\pi).  </math>
The corresponding Young measure satisfies<ref>{{cite book |last1=Dacorogna |first1=Bernard |title=Weak continuity and weak lower semicontinuity of non-linear functionals |date=2006 |publisher=Springer}}</ref>
:<math> \nu_x(E) = \frac{1}{\pi} \int_{E\cap [-1,1]} \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-y^2}} \, \text{d}y, </math>
for any measurable set <math> E </math>, independent of <math>x \in (0,2\pi)</math>.
In other words, for any <math> F \in C(\mathbb{R}^n)</math>:
:<math>F(f_n) {\rightharpoonup}^* \frac{1}{\pi} \int_{-1}^1 \frac{F(y)}{\sqrt{1-y^2}} \, \text{d}y </math> 
in <math>L^\infty((0,2\pi)) </math>. Here, the Young measure does not depend on <math>x</math> and so the weak* limit is always a constant.

To see this intuitively, consider that at the limit of large <math>n</math>, a rectangle of <math>[x, x+\delta x] \times [y, y + \delta y]</math> would capture a part of the curve of <math>f_n</math>. Take that captured part, and project it down to the x-axis. The length of that projection is <math>\frac{2\delta x \delta y}{\sqrt{1-y^2}}</math>, which means that <math>\lim_n f_n</math> should look like a fine mist that has probability density <math>\frac{1}{\pi\sqrt{1-y^2}}</math> at all <math>x</math>.

=== Minimizing sequence ===
For every asymptotically minimizing sequence <math>u_n</math>  of 
:<math>I(u) = \int_0^1 (u'(x)^2-1)^2 +u(x)^2 dx</math>
subject to <math>u(0)=u(1)=0</math> (that is, the sequence satisfies <math>\lim_{n\to+\infty} I(u_n)=\inf_{u\in C^1([0,1])}I(u)</math>), and perhaps after passing to a subsequence, the sequence of derivatives <math>u'_n</math> generates Young measures of the form <math>\nu_x= \frac 12  \delta_{-1} + \frac 12 \delta_1</math>. This captures the essential features of all minimizing sequences to this problem, namely, their derivatives <math>u'_k(x)</math> will tend to concentrate along the minima <math>\{-1,1\}</math> of the integrand <math>(u'(x)^2-1)^2 +u(x)^2</math>.

If we take <math>\lim_n \frac{\sin(2\pi n t)}{2\pi n}</math>, then its limit has value zero, and derivative <math>\nu( dy ) = \frac{1}{\pi\sqrt{1-y^2}}dy</math>, which means <math>\lim I = \frac{1}{\pi}  \int_{-1}^{+1} (1-y^2)^{3/2}dy</math>.
